text.p: The following are the main stories from Thursday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG
- Government ready to force through pensions reform in face of resistance from opposition Social Democrats (SPD).
- Cabinet also agrees pensions reform for civil servants.
- Russian author Lev Kopelev, who made his home in Cologne, dies at age of 85.
- Bundesbank calls for public sector spending cuts.
- Registering European patents to become cheaper, Munich-based European Patent Office says.
HANDELSBLATT
- Employers organisations call for reform to encourage people on welfare benefits to take low-paid jobs.
- Sports car maker Porsche announces joint venture with Harley Davidson.
- Communes should not provide telecommunications services and networks, cabinet says.
- SPD calls for change of orientation in German foreign policy.
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG
- Conference of German protestant church opens with appeal to members to overcome divisons between east and west Germans.
- Finance Minister Theo Waigel's Christian Social Union puts on show of unity as Waigel meets deputies in Bavaria.
- Ifo institute says government target of halving unemployment by the year 2000 is unrealistic.
- Bundesbank council member Christoph Zeitler calls for prospective members of Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) to stick to deficit target of three percent of gross domestic product.
DIE WELT
- No end in sight to row within ruling coalition over how to plug gaps in budget.
- Boost from exports helping German economic growth, Bundesbank says.
- Bundesbank also says German industry has increased its international competitiveness.
- Employment offices start campaign to create more apprenticeships.
